ety.text: From Middle English egle, from Anglo-Norman egle, from Old French aigle, from Latin aquila. Displaced native Middle English ern, earn, arn, from Old English earn (“eagle”). More at erne.

senses.d: Any of several large carnivorous and carrion-eating birds in the family Accipitridae, having a powerful hooked bill and keen vision.
ex:
I, I go my own way
I swim against the stream
Forever I will fight the pοwers that be
The eagle flies alone

senses.d: A gold coin with a face value of ten dollars, formerly used in the United States.
A 13th-century coin minted in Europe and circulated in England as a debased sterling silver penny, outlawed under Edward I of England.
A score of two under par for a hole.
ex: I got an eagle in the third hole.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French aigle, from Old French aigle, itself either borrowed from Old Occitan aigla or taken from Latin aquila, though not as a popular term. Cf. the Old French and regional form aille, which may be popularly inherited. Cognate with Italian aquila, Portuguese águia, Spanish águila, Romanian aceră.
From Latin aquila.
Inherited from Old Spanish aguila. Cognate with French aigle, Italian aquila, Portuguese águia and Romanian aceră.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aguya, from Latin aquila (“eagle”), feminine of aquilus (“dark-coloured”). Doublet of áquila, which was borrowed.
Borrowed from English eagle. Doublet of aigle.

Old French aigrebor. Middle English egre English eager Inherited from Middle English egre, eger, from Old French aigre, egre (modern French aigre), from Latin ācrus, variant of ācer (“sharp, keen”); see acid, acerb, etc. Compare vinegar, alegar.

senses.d: Desirous; keen to do or obtain something.
ex: Stacey is very eager to go cycling this weekend.
The hounds were eager in the chase.

senses.d: Not employing lazy evaluation; calculating results immediately, rather than deferring calculation until they are required.

ex: gold itself will be sometimes so eager, (as artists call it), that it will as little endure the hammer as glass itself
If so thou thinkest, vex him with eager words.
It is a nipping and an eager air.
Our spirits fret and chafe like sea waves on the rocks eagering to climb the shore.
The buggy jolted on, the stout, wellkept team eagering, homing, barning.
His hair crinkled towards her fondly. "Yes," he eagered.

senses.d: To make or encourage to be eager
ex: Physicians also admit to eagering patients to turn to specialised web sites in order to read further.
But they only eagered him to be off .

ety.text: Inherited from Old French desirrous. By surface analysis, désirer + -eux.

ety.text: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιαστής (enthousiastḗs).
Borrowed from Latin impatientem. Morphologically analyzable as im- + patient.
